title: Zacchaeus up a tree (Luke 19:1–10)
hookLine: a short, hated tax collector climbs a sycamore; Jesus invites himself for dinner
last: YOU CAN'T STAY ON THE MOUNTAIN.

lines: THE SHORT KID AT A PARADE.
cards: Ever been the short kid at a parade, seeing nothing but shoulders? Jericho, an old city on the road up to Jerusalem. Jesus is passing through, and the streets are packed.
One man badly wants to see him: Zacchaeus, chief among the publicans, the tax collectors, Luke says, and rich. Before this story ends, the whole crowd will call him a sinner. And he's short.
So a grown, wealthy, powerful, unpopular man runs ahead and does something undignified.

teach.b: Luke says he "climbed up into a sycomore tree to see him: for he was to pass that way." A sycamore fig, a wide, low tree with branches easy to climb, not the American sycamore. A rich official, up a tree like a boy.

teach.h: ZACCHAEUS, MAKE HASTE, AND COME DOWN.
teach.b: Jesus reaches the spot, stops, looks up, and says his name: "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." Luke doesn't say how he knows the name.
And he doesn't wait to be invited; he invites himself to dinner. Zacchaeus scrambles down and welcomes him joyfully.
But the crowd grumbles, all of them, Luke says: "That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner."

teach.h: HALF TO THE POOR, FOURFOLD BACK.
teach.b: Unasked, Zacchaeus stands and says: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." Fourfold.
The law of Moses asked a thief to pay back four sheep for one. He holds himself to the thief's standard, on his own. Notice the order.
Jesus didn't say, change first, then I'll come. He called him by name, came to his house, and the change came after, freely.

teach.h: TO SEEK AND TO SAVE THAT WHICH WAS LOST.
teach.b: Then: "This day is salvation come to this house," and a line some readers take as a summary of Luke's whole Gospel: "For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost."
Some readers also hear a small irony in his name, linking it to a Hebrew word for pure. The whole town called him a sinner. Jesus called him by his name.

how: Many churches read the story of Zacchaeus at the dedication of a church building, and it's a favorite in children's Sunday school, often with a song. Christians often point to it when speaking of restitution: making amends in practical ways.

games.q: you're Zacchaeus. Jesus has just come to your house, and the whole town is grumbling that he's eating with a sinner. what do you do?
o: stand up and promise half your goods to the poor, and fourfold back.
games.why: Zacchaeus stands and promises half to the poor and fourfold to anyone he's cheated. Jesus says: this day is salvation come to this house.

practice: Think of one thing you got wrong with someone, not the worst thing you ever did, but something you could actually fix: money you owe, a broken promise, credit that wasn't yours, a harsh word never taken back.
Picture the person, and what making it right might look like, without beating yourself up; Zacchaeus didn't, he just stood up and said what he'd do. If you pray, you can ask for the courage.

wordCard.voice: Sycamore. A wide, low fig tree, the one a rich, short, unpopular tax collector climbed just to see Jesus pass by.
